title: Projectiles (maths)
examples: How do I find the maximum height of a thrown ball?
What is the formula for the horizontal distance traveled?
Does air resistance affect these calculations?

explain.say: Today we look at projectile motion in mathematics. We will find the components of motion. Think about throwing a ball in the air.
The motion has two parts moving at once. These are the horizontal and the vertical components. We treat them separately for calculation.
The horizontal component moves at a constant velocity. There is no acceleration acting on it in that direction. This is a simple straight line motion.
The vertical component is affected by gravity. Gravity causes a constant downward acceleration. This changes the vertical velocity over time.
Next we find the time of flight. This is the total time the object stays in the air. We find this using the vertical motion equations. The object returns to the starting height.

faq.q: What is the range of a projectile?
faq.a: The range is the total horizontal distance the projectile travels. It is found by multiplying the initial horizontal speed by the total time of flight.
asks: How do I calculate the horizontal distance?
What does range mean in this context?

faq.q: How do I find the greatest height?
faq.a: The greatest height is the maximum vertical displacement from the starting point. At this point, the vertical velocity momentarily becomes zero.
asks: What is the maximum height formula?
When is the object at its peak?

faq.q: Do I need to use trigonometry for the components?
faq.a: Yes, you use sine and cosine to break the initial velocity into its horizontal and vertical parts. Cosine gives the x-component, and sine gives the y-component.
asks: How do I split the initial velocity?

faq.q: Does air resistance change these formulas?
faq.a: These standard formulas assume no air resistance. If air resistance is present, the motion becomes much more complex to calculate.
asks: Are these formulas accurate with wind?

faq.q: What is the initial velocity angle?
faq.a: This is the angle the object is launched above the horizontal ground. It is usually given in degrees or radians.

facts: The horizontal velocity component remains constant if air resistance is ignored.
The vertical motion is always governed by the acceleration due to gravity, g.
The time of flight is determined by the initial vertical velocity.
The maximum height occurs when the vertical velocity component is zero.

quiz.say: A ball is thrown with an initial speed of ten meters per second at an angle of sixty degrees. What is the initial vertical component of velocity?

options.show: ten times the sine of sixty degrees
options.say: ten times the sine of sixty degrees

options.show: ten times the cosine of sixty degrees
options.say: ten times the cosine of sixty degrees

quiz.why: The vertical component uses the sine function because it relates to the height component of the velocity.

wrong.1: Cosine gives the horizontal component, not the vertical one.
wrong.2: You cannot simply multiply the speed by the angle in this formula.
wrong.3: Squaring the speed is incorrect; you must use the sine function.

quiz.say: If an object is launched straight up, what is its horizontal component of velocity?
quiz.why: When launched straight up, there is no horizontal movement, so the horizontal velocity is zero.

wrong.1: The initial speed is the total speed, not just the horizontal part.
wrong.2: Gravity only affects the vertical motion, not the horizontal one.
wrong.3: The initial vertical velocity is not necessarily zero, even if the horizontal velocity is.

quiz.say: A projectile lands at the same height from which it was launched. If the total time of flight is four seconds, what is the initial vertical velocity?

options.show: four times the acceleration due to gravity
options.say: four times the acceleration due to gravity

options.show: the initial vertical velocity multiplied by four
options.say: the initial vertical velocity multiplied by four

quiz.why: Since the final height equals the initial height, the net change in vertical position is zero.

wrong.0: This calculation incorrectly combines time and acceleration directly.
wrong.1: This assumes the vertical velocity remains constant over the entire flight time.
wrong.3: The initial speed is not necessarily zero just because it lands at the same height.
